# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Critical reading of Varga & Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot"

This comment does two different things, and they deserve different verdicts:

- **Sections 1–5** re-analyse the Halden microdata. This part is careful, valuable and mostly convincing.
- **Sections 6–8** argue that the remaining gain is "entirely an artifact". This part overreaches. It relies on speculation, quotes the Varden trial selectively, and contradicts the paper's own data note.

## What checks out

The Table 2 arithmetic is correct:

| Specification | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Record-based output, scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 | +10.8% |

The other figures also check:

- **Hours.** 40.3 → 34.6 is a fall of 14.1%, and 40.4 → 34.8 is a fall of 13.9%.
- **Revenue.** Deflating 1.4% nominal growth by 4.1% inflation (1.014 / 1.041) gives a real fall of about 2.6%.

## What is genuinely valuable

1. **The attrition finding.** This is the most important point in the comment. The working paper said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata show that seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule began, and that six cited workload or output. If accurate, the working paper misdescribed its own sample, and the 61 organisations are survivors.
2. **The manager-versus-records comparison.** The manager's index exceeded the record-based index in 19 of 23 organisations. That is direct evidence for the bias I suspected in the original paper, and it is now measured rather than assumed.
3. **Actual hours.** The time-tracking data quantify the scheduled-hours problem. Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%.
4. **Revenue.** Deflating by inflation is correct and turns nominal "growth" into a real decline.
5. **The data note.** The authors openly say their corrected subsets are non-random. That is good practice.

## Problems in the re-analysis itself

### The abstract overstates what was corrected

The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems brings the gain to 10.8%. The first of those problems is attrition. Table 2, however, corrects only output and hours. Attrition is described but never quantified.

A simple bounding exercise would have helped. For example, the authors could assign the nine withdrawn organisations an output of 80 or 85 and recompute the result. As it stands, the abstract implies a correction that was not performed.

### The hours breakdown doesn't add up

The paper says the gap between scheduled and actual hours has two components:

- +0.7 hours per day on four working days, which is about 2.8 hours a week;
- 1.6 hours a week logged on the day off.

Added to 32 scheduled hours, that gives about 36.4 hours a week. The paper reports 34.6.

Either the components are measured on a different basis or there is an error. If the component figures are correct, actual hours fell by only about 10%, which would strengthen the authors' case. Either way, the discrepancy needs explaining.

### Record-based output may be biased downward

One of the record types listed is **billable hours delivered**. That is a measure of hours, not of output. In organisations that used it, cutting hours lowers the "output" index almost mechanically.

So part of the 3.8-point gap between managers and records could come from this choice of measure rather than from manager optimism. The comparison should be broken down by record type.

### Subsets are small and selected

The main corrected figure rests on 17 organisations that had both time tracking and records. The retail result of −11.2% rests on three organisations. The authors acknowledge this in the data note, but the conclusion then ignores it.

## Where the argument overreaches

### The novelty argument (section 6)

- **Wrong variable.** The decaying measure is self-reported energy, not output. A fall in enthusiasm does not show that the output gain is falling.
- **Two-point extrapolation.** Projecting a decline from just two observations is speculative, and the arithmetic is loose. A fall from 0.61 to 0.29 in three months would reach zero around month 8.7, not month 10. The decline could just as well level off.
- **Burden of proof.** "Not yet shown to be durable" is a reasonable position. Moving from there to "entirely an artifact" is a different and much stronger claim that the evidence does not support.

### Selective use of the Varden trial

The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature". Yet the same randomised trial also found gains in output per actual hour:

| Varden stratum | Gain per actual hour | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| Case-processing | +12.5% | +6.9 to +18.4 |
| Counter and contact centre | +6.7% | +0.4 to +13.3 |

That trial used record-based output, timesheet hours and a control group, and it measured results at nine months. Nine months is around the point where, on the comment's own extrapolation, the novelty effect should have disappeared.

The Varden case-processing figure (+12.5%) also closely matches the comment's own corrected Halden figure (+10.8%). Two very different designs converging on roughly 11–12% is evidence that a modest gain is real. It is not evidence that the gain is an artifact.

### The critique of the meetings analysis (section 7)

This section mischaracterises the Varden analysis.

- **Not a post-hoc subgroup.** The seven offices were not "selected for analysis after the results were known". They are all the treated offices in a stratum that was defined before randomisation.
- **Data timing.** The meeting data were collected in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month outcomes were known.
- **The caveats were already there.** The Varden authors stated that the analysis was unregistered, rested on seven offices, and could not establish a mechanism. They also registered a confirmatory test.
- **Corroborating evidence is ignored.** In the Halden pilot, 47 of 58 managers independently mentioned cutting meetings.

My earlier criticism of the Varden meetings analysis still applies: there is no pre-period baseline for meeting time. But "weak, flagged, and awaiting confirmation" is not the same as "should not be cited".

The meetings mechanism is also an alternative to the novelty explanation. Removing low-value time is a change that could persist. Dismissing it removes the main competitor to the comment's preferred account.

### A conclusion broader than the data

The comment's conclusion goes well beyond what it analysed:

- It analysed one pilot, but its conclusion covers "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" in general.
- Its own data note says the corrected estimates describe only the subsets, not the pilot as a whole.
- It calls the negative counter-office result "the best-supported finding". But the Varden case-processing result is equally well supported: output per employee showed no detectable change, and output per hour rose.

## Bottom line

Sections 1–5 make a strong case that the Halden headline was inflated:

- Attrition was misreported.
- Managers' ratings overstated output.
- Using scheduled hours inflated the per-hour gain.
- Revenue fell in real terms.

On the comment's own corrections, the per-hour gain is roughly halved, to about 11%. Attrition is not yet adjusted for, and there are open questions about the hours components and the billable-hours measure.

The claim that the gain is entirely an artifact does not follow. It rests on extrapolating a self-reported energy measure and dismissing the one randomised trial's per-hour results. That trial independently found a similar gain of about 12.5% at nine months.

Taken together, the three papers support this reading:

- **Per actual hour,** there is a modest gain of about 10–12%, at least over 6–9 months. How long it lasts is unknown.
- **Per employee,** output is maintained only where work isn't tied to presence. In coverage-bound roles, output and service fall.
- **The mechanism,** whether rest, removing low-value time such as meetings, or novelty, is unresolved. The Varden 24-month follow-up is the best test.
